note: Starter scam alerts shown on /alerts alongside the ones posted on /admin. Edit with a commit. Fields match the ScamAlert model: severity is info, warning, or urgent; details has one point per line.

alerts.title: Medicare open enrollment: watch out for “Medicare” callers
alerts.summary: Medicare open enrollment runs from October 15 to December 7, 2026. Scammers call pretending to be from Medicare. They offer a “new card” or a “better plan” and ask for your Medicare number or bank details.
alerts.details:
- Medicare will not call you out of the blue to ask for your Medicare number or bank information.
- Caller ID can be faked to show “Medicare.” Don't trust it.
- Hang up. Then call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227) yourself, using the number on your Medicare card.
- For free, unbiased help comparing plans, contact your State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP).
- Treat your Medicare number like a credit card number.

alerts.title: Texts about “unpaid tolls” are almost always fake
alerts.summary: Scam texts claim you owe money for tolls and must pay right away, even if you haven't driven on a toll road. The link goes to a fake page that steals your card or bank details. The same trick is used in texts about “missed packages.”
alerts.details:
- Don't tap the link and don't reply, not even “STOP.”
- If you're worried, call your toll agency using a number you already know, like the one on your toll account or the back of your toll tag.
- Report the text with your phone's “Report Junk” option, or forward it to 7726 (SPAM). Then delete it.

alerts.title: No real agency will send a courier to pick up your cash or gold
alerts.summary: Scammers pose as tech support, your bank, or a government agency. They say your accounts were hacked and that you must turn your savings into cash or gold “to keep it safe.” Then they send a courier to your door to collect it. The money is never seen again.
alerts.details:
- The government and real businesses will never ask you to buy gold or other precious metals.
- Never hand cash or valuables to a courier or someone you don't know, and don't share your home address.
- Don't call phone numbers that appear in a pop-up, text, or email you weren't expecting.
- Never let someone you don't know take control of your computer.
- Stop and call a family member or your bank, using a number you already know.

alerts.title: Lost money to a scam? Watch out for fake “recovery” helpers
alerts.summary: After someone is scammed, a second scammer often reaches out claiming to be from the FBI's crime complaint center (IC3), a lawyer, or a recovery company. They promise to get your money back for a fee. It's another scam.
alerts.details:
- IC3 never contacts people directly by phone, email, social media, or apps.
- IC3 never charges a fee to recover money, and it doesn't send you to companies that do.
- Don't send money, gift cards, or cryptocurrency to anyone you've met only by phone or online.
- To report a scam, go to ic3.gov yourself.
- If you're 60 or older and want help filing a report, call the DOJ Elder Justice Hotline at 1-833-372-8311.
